findings.topic: Groq vision lineup — only ONE vision model exists
findings.detail: As of Aug 2026 Groq serves exactly one image-capable model: `qwen/qwen3.6-27b`. Groq's vision doc lists it as the sole supported model. It sits in the PREVIEW models table (131,072 context / 16,384 max completion). Production models (llama-3.1-8b-instant, llama-3.3-70b-versatile, openai/gpt-oss-120b, openai/gpt-oss-20b, whisper-*, groq/compound*) are all text/audio only. Legacy IDs `llama-3.2-11b-vision-preview` and `llava-v1.5-7b` are deprecated/removed. Verify live via GET https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/models.

findings.topic: "gemini-3.5-flash-lite" is real but is NOT a Groq model
findings.detail: The sibling project's two references resolve to DIFFERENT providers. `qwen/qwen3.6-27b` IS on Groq. `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` is a Google model (released 2026-07-21 alongside Gemini 3.6 Flash and 3.5 Flash Cyber), served via Google's Gemini API / Vertex, not Groq. It has a 1,048,576-token context, 65,536 max output, $0.30/M input (text/image/video/audio) and $2.50/M output, defaults to MINIMAL thinking, and is explicitly positioned for "high-throughput classification, routing, or JSON extraction" and document parsing. So the sibling codebase is calling two different vendors — do not assume one Groq key covers both.

findings.topic: BLOCKER: Groq's vision model is rate-limited to 8,000 TPM
findings.detail: On the Developer (paid) plan, `qwen/qwen3.6-27b` limits are 30 RPM, 1,000 RPD, 8,000 TPM, 200,000 TPD. 8,000 tokens/minute is extremely small for vision — a single full-page form image consumes a large fraction of that, so realistic throughput is roughly 1–2 form scans per minute and ~1,000 requests/day hard ceiling. For a multi-tenant form digitization platform doing multi-pass extraction, this is a hard architectural blocker, not a tuning problem. Rate-limit headers: x-ratelimit-remaining-requests/-tokens, x-ratelimit-reset-*, retry-after on 429.

findings.topic: BLOCKER: Groq's vision model does NOT support strict structured outputs
findings.detail: Groq's structured-outputs doc lists strict mode (`strict: true`, json_schema) as supported ONLY on `openai/gpt-oss-20b` and `openai/gpt-oss-120b`; best-effort adds `openai/gpt-oss-safeguard-20b`. All three are TEXT-ONLY. `qwen/qwen3.6-27b` is not listed. Additionally "Streaming and tool use are not currently supported with Structured Outputs." Net effect: on Groq you cannot get schema-guaranteed JSON out of an image. You get only best-effort JSON object mode, which must be defensively parsed and validated. Strict-mode schema rules when it does apply: all fields `required`, all objects `additionalProperties: false`, `anyOf` and `$ref`/`$defs` supported.

findings.topic: Groq qwen3.6-27b pricing and image limits (with a documentation conflict)
findings.detail: Pricing $0.60/M input, $3.00/M output — note the unusual 5x output premium. ~500 tokens/sec. Supports text+image in, tool use, JSON object mode, reasoning (thinking/non-thinking). CONFLICT: the model page states "Maximum 3 input images per request" while the vision doc states "You can process a maximum of 5 images". Both agree on 20MB max request size for image URL input. Max base64 size and max pixel resolution are NOT documented anywhere I could find. Benchmarks quoted: GPQA Diamond 87.8%, AIME 2026 94.1%, SWE-bench Verified 77.2%. Model is Apache 2.0, released 2026-04-22, 27B dense, available from ~10 providers with cheapest at ~$0.289/M input — Groq is not the low-cost route for it.

findings.topic: Groq preview-model discontinuation risk is documented and real
findings.detail: Groq labels preview models as for evaluation, not production, and can discontinue at short notice. Precedent: on 2026-07-21 Groq removed Llama 4 Scout and Qwen3 32B from both the rate card and the docs catalog. Since `qwen/qwen3.6-27b` is Groq's ONLY vision model AND is preview-status, a Groq-only vision path is a single point of failure with no in-provider fallback.

findings.topic: Gemini bounding-box convention — EXACT and load-bearing
findings.detail: Gemini returns `box_2d` as [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] — y-FIRST — normalized to 0–1000. Official wording: "The coordinates, relative to image dimensions, scale to [0, 1000]" and "The box_2d should be [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] normalized to 0-1000." Coordinates map (0,0,1000,1000) onto (0,0,width,height). Segmentation masks are returned as a polygon of [x,y] points also normalized 0–1000, each with a bounding box, label and contour. Object detection/segmentation is called out as having extra training on gemini-3.7-flash. Trigger the behaviour with an explicit prompt like "Detect the 2D bounding boxes of the ...".

findings.topic: Gemini bbox accuracy is highly sensitive to coordinate ORDER and to thinking budget
findings.detail: Two empirically documented failure modes. (1) Format sensitivity: the model is tuned so heavily on yxyx that switching to (xmin,ymin,xmax,ymax) causes performance to "tank"; a 2026 video-grounding benchmark reproduced this — both prompt variants scored much higher when parsed as yxyx. (2) Thinking hurts: in an mAP evaluation of Gemini 2.5, Google's own docs recommend turning the thinking budget OFF for detection, and results supported it. Roboflow100-VL methodology used native-resolution images, a system prompt demanding a JSON array with labels and no masks/code fences, and capped output at 8192 tokens.

findings.topic: Qwen uses the OPPOSITE axis order to Gemini — xyxy, not yxyx
findings.detail: Qwen3-VL (and by lineage Qwen3.6) returns `bbox_2d` as [x1, y1, x2, y2] — x-FIRST, top-left then bottom-right — normalized 0–1000. Qwen3-VL moved to normalized 0–1000, unlike Qwen2.5-VL which used absolute pixels of the resized image. Pixel conversion: x1 = box[0]/1000*w, y1 = box[1]/1000*h, etc. A benchmark comparing three conventions found 1000-base most robust: Qwen3-VL-8B scored 24.54 with 1000-base coords, 5.46 with unit-scale [0,1], and 0 with absolute pixels. CRITICAL: mixing up Gemini's yxyx with Qwen's xyxy silently transposes every box — on a portrait A4 form that puts the photo box in completely the wrong place.

findings.topic: Claude uses a THIRD convention — absolute pixels, and explicitly warns against normalized
findings.detail: Anthropic has a dedicated docs page. Claude returns absolute pixel coordinates, origin (0,0) top-left, x right, y down, as [x1,y1,x2,y2]. Verbatim: "Claude works best with absolute pixel coordinates. Ask for them explicitly in your prompt... Claude does not work well when you ask for normalized coordinates, for example: 'Return bounding box coordinates between 0 and 1000.' Always ask for pixel coordinates and normalize in your own code if you need to." So all three families differ: Gemini yxyx/0-1000, Qwen xyxy/0-1000, Claude xyxy/absolute-pixels.

findings.topic: Claude's image resize math — the #1 documented cause of misaligned coordinates
findings.detail: Claude returns coordinates in the space of the image AFTER its own resize. Rule: largest aspect-preserving size where (a) neither side exceeds max edge, and (b) visual token cost ceil(w/28)*ceil(h/28) is within budget. Standard tier: 1568 px edge / 1568 tokens. High-resolution tier (Claude 4.7 and later): 2576 px / 4784 tokens. The TOKEN limit usually binds, not the edge limit — docs give the exact trap: an A4 scan at 130 DPI is 1075x1520, both sides under 1568, but costs 39*55 = 2145 tokens, so it is resized to 924x1307 on standard tier (and NOT resized at all on high-res tier). Claude then pads to the next multiple of 28 on bottom/right only — always rescale by RESIZED dims, never padded dims. Anthropic ships a reference `resizedSize()` implementation in TypeScript (uses banker's rounding to match the live API). Best practice: pre-resize yourself so coordinates map 1:1, and set `"transformations": {"oversized_image": "error"}` on the image block to turn silent server-side resizing into a 400 error that names the exact target dimensions.

findings.topic: Claude's own documented spatial limitations
findings.detail: Verbatim from the Vision limitations list: "Spatial reasoning: Claude's coordinate and localization outputs are approximate. Follow the guidance in Coordinates and bounding boxes and verify outputs before relying on them." Also "Accuracy: Claude might hallucinate or make mistakes when interpreting low-quality, rotated, or very small images under 200 pixels." The coordinates page adds: "Small elements lose precision when an image is downscaled: for fine targets, crop the region of interest and send the crop (offset returned coordinates by the crop origin), or use a high-resolution-tier model." That crop-then-offset pattern is directly applicable to a template-registered pipeline.

findings.topic: RISK for passport-photo handling: Claude refuses person identification
findings.detail: Documented limitation: "People identification: Claude cannot be used to name people in images and refuses to do so." Detecting and cropping a photograph REGION is not identification and should be fine, but prompts must be worded as geometric/document tasks ("locate the rectangular pasted photograph region") and never as anything resembling identifying or describing the person. Also note images are ephemeral, deleted after processing, and not used for training — relevant for health/insurance PII compliance.

findings.topic: Handwriting OCR: line-level leaderboards are misleading for your use case
findings.detail: Two very different pictures. Clean line-level IAM: GPT-5 ~1.22% CER, Claude Opus 4.7 ~1.31%, Gemini 3 ~1.44%; specialist DTrOCR 2.38%, TrOCR-Large 2.89%; Azure Document Intelligence v4.0 ~1.8% CER cited as best accuracy+structured-output combination. Full-page multilingual handwritten documents (METATR): Gemini 3 Pro best at 28.5% CER handwritten (17.6% printed), Claude Opus 4.5 second at 31.2%. That is a ~20x gap between line-level and real full-page handwriting. Also: preprocessing choices (case folding, whitespace) shift CER by 5–15%, so fix your protocol before comparing. Practitioner reports of ~84% on clean handwritten sections dropping to ~70% on messy handwritten comments.

findings.topic: Devanagari: the only rigorous 2026 benchmark — and it is PRINTED text only
findings.detail: arXiv 2606.29213, "Can OCR-VLMs Read Devanagari? A Stress-Test Benchmark and Post-Correction Study" (submitted 2026-06-28). Ten systems, four synthetic degradations, 300 REAL PRINTED scans. On clean rendered text all ten cluster chrF++ 91–98 — i.e. synthetic renders are useless for discrimination. On real scans nine of ten collapse across a 76-point spread: Gemini 2.5 Flash 86.3, Claude Opus 4.7 82.2, Qwen3-VL-8B 75.2, GPT-5.5 58.5, EasyOCR 58.3 (down from 93.6), olmOCR-7B 40.5. Key lesson: strong English OCR does NOT predict Indic OCR. Their error taxonomy separates surface errors (numerals, punctuation) from structural ones (conjuncts, matras, nukta) — the structural class is what breaks Devanagari. NOTE: this covers printed Devanagari, NOT handwriting, so treat these as an optimistic upper bound for your case.

findings.topic: No published benchmark exists for handwritten Indian names on forms
findings.detail: This intersection is genuinely under-served. The Indic handwriting datasets (IIIT-HW-Dev: ~95,381 word samples but only 12 writers; IIIT-Indic-HW-Words; CHIPS/PLATTER page-level; DohaScript 2026 continuous handwritten Hindi) predate or exclude VLM evaluation. The 2026 VLM Devanagari benchmark covers printed text only. Proper nouns are specifically hard because language-model priors and lexicon decoding help far less than on ordinary vocabulary — and prior Indic work often relied on lexicon-based decoding that will not generalize to arbitrary Indian names. You will have to build your own labelled eval set; there is no shortcut.

findings.topic: Azure Document Intelligence: per-WORD confidence + polygon + isHandwritten flag — best fit for confidence scoring
findings.detail: `prebuilt-read` (v4.0 GA, api-version 2024-11-30) returns for each word: `content`, `polygon` (bounding polygon coords), `confidence` (e.g. 0.997), and `span`. Separately a `styles` collection returns `isHandwritten: true` WITH its own `confidence` (e.g. 0.95) and spans pointing at the text range. That handwritten-style flag is directly valuable for your product: it separates pre-printed form labels from the staff-filled handwritten values automatically. Input limits: 500 MB paid (S0) / 4 MB free (F0); image dims must be 50x50 to 10,000x10,000 px; min text height 12 px at 1024x768 (~8pt at 150 DPI); up to 2,000 pages per PDF/TIFF.

findings.topic: BLOCKER: Azure handwriting does NOT support Hindi/Devanagari
findings.detail: Azure v4.0 handwritten-text language support is exactly 12 languages: English, Chinese Simplified, French, German, Italian, Thai, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, Russian, Arabic. Hindi is absent. Hindi (`hi`), Marathi (`mr`), Sanskrit (`sa`) and ~20 other Devanagari-script languages ARE supported for PRINTED text only. Same 12-language handwriting list applies to `prebuilt-layout`. So Azure can read your printed Hindi form labels but cannot read handwritten Devanagari values. Also note: Azure docs advise NOT passing a language code unless certain — "the service may return incomplete and incorrect text" if you force the wrong model.

findings.topic: Azure Document Intelligence pricing
findings.detail: S0 pay-as-you-go, verified against Microsoft's Azure Retail Prices API (East US): Read (OCR) $1.50/1,000 pages; Layout $10/1K; prebuilt models $10/1K; custom extraction $30/1K; document classifier $3/1K; query fields $10/1K; add-ons $6/1K each. Base operations are NOT double-billed — 1,000 Layout pages cost $10, not $11.50. No batch discount (batch metered identically to sync). Commitment tiers cut Read to $0.45/1K but are not shown on the main pricing page. Free F0 tier: 500 pages/month, but returns only the first 2 pages per request and caps at 1 TPS. India-region (Central/South India) rates NOT verified — pricing does vary by region.

findings.topic: AWS Textract has a purpose-built SIGNATURES detector — highly relevant and very cheap
findings.detail: `AnalyzeDocument` FeatureTypes valid values: TABLES | FORMS | QUERIES | SIGNATURES | LAYOUT. Per AWS API docs: "Signatures. A SIGNATURE Block object contains the location information of a signature in a document. If used in conjunction with forms or tables, a signature can be given a Key-Value pairing or be detected in the cell of a table." Every Block carries `Geometry.BoundingBox` (normalized Left/Top/Width/Height), `Geometry.Polygon` (X/Y points), `Geometry.RotationAngle`, and `Confidence`. It detects handwritten signatures, electronic signatures AND initials. Price: $0.0035/page first 1M, $0.0014/page above = $3.50 per 1,000 pages — by far the cheapest AnalyzeDocument feature (Forms is $50/1K, Tables $15/1K). Free tier is 1,000 pages/month for Signatures vs only 100 for Forms/Tables. CRITICAL INSIGHT: signature detection is a VISUAL detector, so it is script-agnostic — it works on Indian forms even though Textract's handwriting OCR is English-only.

findings.topic: AWS Textract per-word confidence and handwriting flag
findings.detail: WORD blocks return `Text`, `TextType` (PRINTED | HANDWRITING), `Confidence` (0–100, "the probability that a prediction is correct"), and `Geometry` (normalized BoundingBox + Polygon; multiply by image w/h to draw). Documented example: `"Text": "Name:", "TextType": "PRINTED", "BlockType": "WORD", "Confidence": 99.56`. AWS suggests flagging anything below ~95%. `DetectDocumentText` alone ($0.0015/page = $1.50/1K) already gives words + confidence + bbox + handwriting type — you do NOT need AnalyzeDocument for that, a >40x cost difference vs Forms. Limits: sync max 10 MB, async max 500 MB PDF; PNG/JPEG/PDF/TIFF only. Mumbai (ap-south-1) is priced identically to N. Virginia since the 2021 reduction.

findings.topic: BLOCKER: AWS Textract supports NO Indian language, and handwriting is English-only
findings.detail: Textract printed-text languages are exactly six: English, Spanish, German, Italian, French, Portuguese. Handwriting recognition (launched Nov 2020) is English ONLY — the five additional languages were added for PRINTED text only. Devanagari is in neither list. There is no language-selection parameter and Textract does not return detected language. The June 2025 model refresh added superscripts/subscripts/rotated text and low-resolution accuracy but added NO languages. Textract is therefore viable for your SIGNATURES/geometry needs and for English handwriting, but not for Hindi text at all.

findings.topic: Google Document AI: token-level confidence + normalized vertices, pricing
findings.detail: Document AI returns a `layout` object per element containing `textAnchor.textSegments`, `confidence`, `boundingPoly.normalizedVertices` (x/y floats), and `orientation` (e.g. PAGE_UP). This layout pattern repeats down the page hierarchy (blocks, paragraphs, lines, TOKENS), so token-level confidence + bbox is available. Enterprise Document OCR supports language hints AND handwriting hints via OCR config, on pretrained-ocr-v2.0-2023-06-02, v2.1-2024-08-07 and RC v2.1.1-2025-01-31. Selection-mark (checkbox/radio) detection is available via `ProcessOptions.ocrConfig.premiumFeatures.enableSelectionMarkDetection`, surfacing in `Document.pages[].visualElements[]` as unfilled_checkbox/filled_checkbox — directly useful for your checkbox/radio field types. Pricing: Enterprise Document OCR $1.50/1K pages (1–5M/mo), $0.60/1K above 5M; OCR add-ons $6/1K; Custom Extractor and Form Parser $30/1K (1–1M/mo), $20/1K above; Layout Parser $10/1K; custom processor hosting $0.05/deployed-version-hour. Not billed for 4xx/5xx failures. No free tier beyond the $300 new-customer credit.

findings.topic: COULD NOT VERIFY: Google Document AI handwriting language coverage
findings.detail: The Document AI supported-languages page presents a "Handwriting supported" column across Enterprise Document OCR, Custom Extractor, Form Parser and Layout Parser, but in the fetched rendering EVERY entry in that column read as blank — including Hindi, which is listed for printed support. I could not determine whether this means (a) no language has handwriting support in that table, (b) the column failed to render its checkmarks through the markdown conversion, or (c) handwriting support is gated behind the separate handwriting-hint OCR config rather than the language table. Third-party comparison sites do list Google Document AI as having handwriting support, but none specify Devanagari. This needs a direct check in a browser before any architecture decision depends on it.

findings.topic: Gemini logprobs: real, but gated per-model and absent from the OpenAI compat layer
findings.detail: Controlled by `generationConfig.responseLogprobs: true` plus optional integer `logprobs` (number of top candidates). Response candidates carry `avgLogprobs` (double) and `logprobsResult` containing `topCandidates` (arrays of token/logProbability pairs) and `chosenCandidates`. Availability is gated per model, not family-wide — one developer hit `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT: Logprobs is not enabled for models/gemini-2.5-flash` after it had worked the day before. NOT supported through Gemini's OpenAI-compatibility layer (fails with unknown-field error). Third-party SDKs lag: open feature requests against both LiteLLM and the Vercel AI SDK's Google provider. Logprobs apply to OUTPUT tokens so they should be modality-independent, but I could not find a doc or report confirming logprobs on a current Gemini VISION call specifically.

findings.topic: OpenAI logprobs with image input: works in practice, with caveats
findings.detail: `logprobs` / `top_logprobs` are documented on Chat Completions (top-5 by default, expandable). Strongest evidence for multimodal use is research usage: a published pipeline feeds an image to GPT-4o and requests the top 14 logits, renormalizing across classes — confirming output-token logprobs work alongside image inputs, since logprobs attach to generated tokens regardless of input modality. Two unverified gotchas: reasoning models have historically restricted logprobs support (GPT-5 reasoning variants may reject the parameter), and parameter support diverges between the Responses API and Chat Completions. Cheapest resolution is an empirical test call with an input_image plus logprobs:true, top_logprobs:5.

findings.topic: No provider exposes logprobs for image INPUT tokens
findings.detail: Output-token logprobs are the only thing available anywhere. Input/prompt logprobs for multimodal input are not exposed: OpenAI's chat endpoints have never exposed input-token logprobs at all, and a vLLM issue documents that while `prompt_logprobs`/`echo` work on `/completions`, multimodal models route through `/chat/completions` which does not parse them. Anthropic exposes no logprobs parameter at all — I found no logprobs support in the Claude API docs. Practical consequence: you cannot get a calibrated "how confident is the model that this pixel region is a photograph" score from any VLM. VLM-reported confidence is self-reported text, not a probability — it is uncalibrated and should not be trusted for your low-confidence-review gating.

findings.topic: Gemini image input limits and the media_resolution control
findings.detail: Max 3,600 image files per request. Token cost: images with both dims <=384 px cost 258 tokens; larger images are tiled into 768x768 tiles at 258 tokens each (crop unit ~ floor(min(w,h)/1.5)). Gemini 3 replaced Pan-and-Scan with variable sequence length tokenization. `media_resolution` (Gemini 3) caps tokens per image with levels low / medium / high / ultra_high; ultra_high is per-content-item only and recommended for computer use. PDFs default to medium (~560 tokens) because "quality typically saturates there and high rarely improves OCR on standard documents". Per-part media resolution is experimental and v1beta only. Size limits CONFLICT: image-understanding docs still state 20MB total inline request size, but a 2026-01-12 Google announcement raised inline payload from 20MB to 100MB. Treat 20MB as the safe assumption and use the File API above that. Prompting tips: verify correct rotation, and place the text prompt BEFORE the image for single-image requests.

findings.topic: Claude image limits and cost, for capacity planning
findings.detail: Max dims 8000x8000 px. Max size 10 MB base64 direct API (5 MB on Bedrock/Vertex). Max images: 100/request for 200k-context models, 600/request otherwise, 20 on claude.ai. Above 20 image blocks per request a stricter per-image dimension cap kicks in — keep each image <=2000 px per side or keep the request to <=20 image/document blocks. Request size cap 32 MB standard endpoints. Formats JPEG/PNG/GIF/WebP (first frame only). Token cost ceil(w/28)*ceil(h/28). Worked costs from the docs: a 1000x1000 image is 1296 tokens ≈ $1.30/1,000 images on Haiku 4.5 ($1/M), ≈ $6.48/1,000 on Opus 5 ($5/M); a 4K image on high-res tier is 4784 tokens ≈ $23.92/1,000. High-res tier can cost ~3x the visual tokens of standard for the same image. Warning worth heeding for your pipeline: "heavy JPEG compression can make text difficult to read" and repeated compression passes are specifically called out as harmful.

findings.topic: Current Gemini model IDs and pricing (Aug 2026)
findings.detail: Stable: `gemini-3.7-flash` (new stable, "complex coding, agentic workflows, reliable multi-step execution"), `gemini-3.6-flash` (stable), `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` (stable, fastest/cheapest). Preview: `gemini-3.1-pro-preview`. Legacy stable: `gemini-2.5-pro`. Specialized spatial models: `gemini-robotics-er-2-preview` (built on Gemini 3.5 Flash; spatial primitives are pointing, tracking, bounding boxes, trajectories) and `gemini-robotics-er-1.6-preview`. Pricing per 1M: 3.7-flash and 3.6-flash both $0.75 in / $3.75 out through 2026-12-31 then $1.50/$7.50; 3.5-flash-lite $0.30 in / $2.50 out (batch $0.15/$1.25); 3.1-pro-preview $2.00 in (<=200k) / $12.00 out, rising to $4.00/$18.00 above 200k, no free tier. Batch tier is a flat 50% discount.

findings.topic: Hybrid detector+VLM beats VLM-only detection — quantified
findings.detail: Two independent signals that a VLM should not be your primary localizer. (1) In a remote-sensing study Gemini's MAE dropped from 103.81 to 10.72 on degraded images when bounding boxes were SUPPLIED as context rather than predicted — a ~10x error reduction from giving the model geometry instead of asking for it. (2) The Roboflow100-VL conclusion was that CNNs remain faster, cheaper and easier to reason about given good training data, and that Gemini's value is open-set versatility, not precision. Also relevant: Gemini models are not explicitly trained for object detection the way purpose-built PaliGemma is. Encouraging counter-signal for documents specifically: a 2026 walkthrough of scanned-document illustration detection reported "very precise" boxes with no false positives and no false negatives, and correct abstention (empty caption field) on a negative case — which maps well onto your "Not Detected" requirement.

recommendations: Do NOT build the photo/signature pipeline on Groq. Groq has exactly one vision model (qwen/qwen3.6-27b), it is PREVIEW status with documented precedent for sudden removal, it is capped at 8,000 TPM / 1,000 RPD on the paid Developer plan, and it does NOT support strict JSON schema (only text-only gpt-oss models do). Any one of those is disqualifying for a production form platform; together they are decisive. Keep Groq only as an optional fast-path for low-stakes text fields, behind a feature flag, with a non-Groq fallback.

Treat the sibling project's two model IDs as two different vendors. `qwen/qwen3.6-27b` is Groq; `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` is Google's Gemini API. Do not assume the existing Groq key covers both — you will need a separate Google AI/Vertex credential, and it must stay server-side (Vercel env var, never NEXT_PUBLIC_).

Use AWS Textract SIGNATURES as the primary signature detector. It is a purpose-built visual detector returning SIGNATURE blocks with normalized BoundingBox + Polygon + Confidence, it detects handwritten signatures/e-signatures/initials, and it costs $3.50 per 1,000 pages. Crucially it is script-agnostic, so it works on Hindi/English mixed Indian forms despite Textract's OCR being English-only. This directly answers 'a VLM asked for coordinates and hoped' — it is a real detector with a real calibrated confidence score.

Do NOT use a VLM as the primary localizer for the pasted passport photograph. Exploit your stated key advantage instead: the photo is a high-contrast quadrilateral at a KNOWN location in a FIXED template. The right architecture is homography registration of the scan against the stored blank template (from admin upload / staff corrections), then classical edge+corner detection constrained to the registered photo-box ROI. That is a geometry problem solvable in pure TypeScript over sharp's raw pixel buffers — no VLM, no 10MB WASM, deterministic, and it degrades to 'Not Detected' cleanly when the ROI contains no quadrilateral. Reserve the VLM for adjudicating ambiguous cases only.

If you do use VLM grounding as a secondary/fallback signal, get the three coordinate conventions exactly right and encode them as separate typed adapters — they are mutually incompatible. Gemini: box_2d = [ymin, xmin, ymax, xmax] normalized 0-1000. Qwen: bbox_2d = [x1, y1, x2, y2] normalized 0-1000. Claude: [x1, y1, x2, y2] in ABSOLUTE PIXELS of the post-resize image. Transposing Gemini's yxyx as xyxy is silent and catastrophic on portrait A4 forms. Add a unit test per adapter using a synthetic image with a known-position rectangle.

For Gemini detection calls specifically: disable the thinking budget (Google's own docs recommend it and an mAP study confirmed it), send native-resolution images, prompt with the exact documented phrasing 'Detect the 2D bounding boxes of the ...', and demand a JSON array with no code fences or masks. These are documented, measured accuracy factors, not style preferences.

For Claude calls, pre-resize images yourself using Anthropic's published resizedSize() reference implementation and set "transformations": {"oversized_image": "error"} on every coordinate-bearing image block. Otherwise a model-tier change or a new camera source silently reintroduces server-side resizing and shifts every coordinate. Remember Claude 4.7+ is high-res tier (2576 px / 4784 tokens) while older models are standard (1568/1568) — using the wrong tier's limits recovers the wrong dimensions and misaligns everything.

Source per-field confidence from Azure Document Intelligence prebuilt-read (or Textract), NOT from the VLM. Azure returns real per-WORD confidence plus a polygon, AND a styles[].isHandwritten flag with its own confidence — which additionally separates pre-printed form labels from staff-filled handwriting for free. No provider exposes logprobs for image input tokens, and Anthropic exposes no logprobs at all, so a VLM's self-reported '0.85 confidence' is uncalibrated generated text. Do not gate your manual-review screen on it.

Plan for the fact that NO document-AI vendor supports handwritten Devanagari. Azure handwriting is 12 languages (English, zh-Hans, fr, de, it, th, ja, ko, pt, es, ru, ar) — no Hindi. Textract handwriting is English only. Google's handwriting coverage could not be verified. For handwritten Hindi values you must route to a frontier VLM (Gemini led at chrF++ 86.3, Claude 82.2 on real printed Devanagari scans) and set user expectations accordingly — and note those are PRINTED-text numbers, so handwritten Devanagari will be materially worse.

Build your own labelled eval set before choosing models — this is non-negotiable and is the single highest-value engineering investment here. There is no published benchmark for handwritten Indian names on forms. The 2026 Devanagari benchmark showed all ten systems cluster at chrF++ 91-98 on clean synthetic renders but spread across 76 points on real scans, so evaluating on synthetic data will actively mislead you. Collect 100-200 real phone photos of real filled forms across your degradation conditions (skew, glare, crease, photocopy, low light) and label photo/signature/thumb boxes plus field values.

Exploit client-side preprocessing hard, since it is free compute and directly improves every downstream number. Do perspective de-skew, illumination normalization and glare suppression in the browser via canvas/WebGL before upload. This shrinks uploads, keeps you under Groq/Gemini/Claude size limits, and matters more than model choice: Azure requires min text height 12 px at 1024x768 (~8pt at 150 DPI), and Anthropic explicitly warns heavy JPEG compression makes text unreadable and that repeated compression passes compound the damage.

Skip opencv-wasm / @techstark/opencv-js on the Vercel serverless side. Given template registration reduces the problem to a known ROI, the CV you actually need (homography from 4 template anchors, Otsu threshold, connected components, quadrilateral fit, ink-density scoring for thumb impressions) is a few hundred lines of focused TypeScript over sharp raw buffers. That keeps the bundle small and cold starts fast in bom1. If you later need full OpenCV, put it in the browser where the 10MB WASM is amortized across a user session, not in a per-request serverless bundle.

Resolve three specific unknowns before finalizing: (1) whether Groq's per-request image cap is 3 (model page) or 5 (vision doc) — the docs contradict each other; (2) Google Document AI's handwriting language table, which must be checked in a real browser since the 'Handwriting supported' column rendered blank for every language including Hindi; (3) whether logprobs work on a current Gemini vision model — test empirically with responseLogprobs:true on a real image call, since support is gated per-model and absent from the OpenAI compat layer.

Word prompts for photo detection as purely geometric document tasks ('locate the rectangular pasted photograph region and return its bounds'), never as anything resembling describing or identifying the person. Claude refuses person identification by policy, and phrasing that drifts toward identification risks refusals on a core product path. Cropping a region is fine; the prompt must make that unambiguous.
caveats: Google Document AI handwriting language support is UNVERIFIED and is a live gap in this research. The official supported-languages page renders a 'Handwriting supported' column in which every entry — including Hindi — appeared blank through markdown conversion. I could not distinguish 'no handwriting support at all' from a rendering failure from 'gated behind the OCR handwriting-hint config'. Check this in a real browser before relying on Google for any handwriting path.

Groq's own documentation contradicts itself on images per request: the qwen3.6-27b model page says maximum 3 input images, the vision doc says maximum 5. Neither documents a max base64 payload size or a max pixel resolution — only the 20MB image-URL request cap. Test empirically.

No accuracy benchmark exists for AWS Textract SIGNATURES on Indian forms, or for signature/passport-photo detection generally. My recommendation to use it rests on documented capability (SIGNATURE blocks with BoundingBox + Confidence), price, and script-agnosticism — not on measured accuracy in your domain. It must be validated against your own eval set.

The Devanagari VLM numbers (Gemini 86.3, Claude 82.2, Qwen3-VL-8B 75.2, GPT-5.5 58.5 chrF++) are for PRINTED text on real scans, not handwriting. They are an optimistic upper bound for your handwritten use case, and the gap is likely large — the same paper's own framing is that structural features (conjuncts, matras, nukta, shirorekha) are what break Devanagari, and all of those degrade further in handwriting.

Azure India-region (Central India / South India) pricing was NOT verified. The figures quoted are East US, verified against Microsoft's Azure Retail Prices API. Azure Document Intelligence pricing does vary by region. AWS Mumbai (ap-south-1) parity with N. Virginia is from a 2021 AWS announcement and should be re-confirmed on the current pricing page, which did not itself list Mumbai.

Several handwriting-OCR comparison numbers (IAM CER figures, METATR full-page CER, OCR Arena rankings) come from third-party aggregator and blog sources rather than primary papers I fetched directly. Treat the relative ordering as more reliable than the absolute values, and note the sources themselves warn that preprocessing choices shift CER by 5-15%.

Gemini logprobs support on a CURRENT vision model is unconfirmed. The parameters (responseLogprobs, logprobs) and response shape (avgLogprobs, logprobsResult) are documented, and logprobs attach to output tokens so should be modality-independent in principle — but support is gated per-model with reports of it being enabled and then disabled, and I found no report of it working on a Gemini 3.x vision call specifically.

Qwen3.6-27B's exact bounding-box convention is INFERRED from the Qwen3-VL lineage, not confirmed from an official Qwen3.6 model card. One source (PyImageSearch, describing Qwen2.5-VL) implies absolute pixels while the Qwen3-VL-Seg paper describes normalized 0-1000 — and Qwen2.5-VL genuinely did use absolute coordinates. If you use Qwen3.6 for grounding, empirically calibrate against a synthetic test image before trusting either interpretation.

Groq's rate limits and pricing were read from docs at a single point in time on a PREVIEW model. Both can change without notice, and Groq has removed preview models from the rate card and catalog without warning before. Re-verify before any capacity or cost commitment.

Model lineups in this space change on a scale of weeks. Everything here reflects late August 2026. The Gemini 3.7-flash/3.6-flash promotional pricing in particular has a hard documented expiry: rates double on 2027-01-01 ($0.75/$3.75 becomes $1.50/$7.50).

findings.topic: sharp 0.35.3 — cannot do perspective warp (hard blocker for dewarping)
findings.detail: sharp is at 0.35.3 (Apache-2.0, published 2026-07-01, 958 KB unpacked, 89M downloads/wk). Its `affine(matrix, {background, idx, idy, odx, ody, interpolator})` exposes libvips `vips_affine` and accepts a **2x2 matrix only** — it is mathematically incapable of a projective/homography transform. The PR author who added it (lovell/sharp#2336) confirmed it "can only make affine transformations", and maintainer lovell restated in #3071 that "3-point affine transformation is supported via the affine API, but 4-point projection is not". The canonical feature request lovell/sharp#2095 has been open since Feb 2020. libvips itself CAN do it via `vips_mapim` (arbitrary source-coordinate remap), but sharp does not expose mapim. Document-relevant primitives sharp DOES have: resize kernels nearest/linear/cubic/mitchell/lanczos2/lanczos3/mks2013/mks2021; rotate(angle,{background}) (arbitrary angle); autoOrient(); extract(); extend(); flip/flop; normalise({lower:1,upper:99}) percentile stretch; clahe({width,height,maxSlope:3}); linear(a,b); recomb(3x3|4x4); convolve({width,height,kernel,scale,offset}); threshold(t,{greyscale}); boolean(operand,'and'|'or'|'eor',{raw}); median(size); blur({sigma,precision,minAmplitude}); sharpen({sigma,m1,m2,x1,y2,y3}); dilate(width)/erode(width); gamma(); negate(); flatten()/unflatten(); modulate(); removeAlpha/ensureAlpha(alpha)/extractChannel('red'|'green'|'blue'|'alpha'|n)/joinChannel/bandbool; raw({depth:'uchar'|'float'|...}) and sharp(buf,{raw:{width,height,channels}}) for zero-copy raw pixel in/out; toBuffer({resolveWithObject:true}) returning {data, info:{format,size,width,height,channels,premultiplied,cropOffsetLeft,cropOffsetTop}}.

findings.topic: sharp `trim()` — what the algorithm actually is, and why it will not find a pasted photo
findings.detail: Signature: `trim({background, threshold: 10, lineArt: false, margin: 0})`. Background defaults to the top-left pixel. It wraps libvips `find_trim`, which computes a single bounding box of the region NOT similar to the background colour, scanning inward from all four EDGES only; pixels are compared against the background with the given per-channel threshold, and for images with alpha it unions the alpha and colour bounding boxes. If trimming would remove the whole image it is a no-op. The resulting offsets come back on `info.trimOffsetLeft` / `info.trimOffsetTop`. Critically: this is a single global edge-crop, not a content/blob detector — it cannot locate a photograph pasted in the middle of a form, and on a phone photo of a form it will return essentially the whole frame because the shadowed/noisy border is never 'similar to background'. It is only useful for tightening an already-isolated crop (e.g. shrink-wrapping a signature crop onto its ink).

findings.topic: @techstark/opencv-js 5.0.0-release.1 IS practical on Vercel — I benchmarked it
findings.detail:
Apache-2.0. Published 2026-06-24 (actively maintained; 4.12.0 → 5.0.0 upgrade Nov 2025 → Jun 2026). 137,530 downloads/wk. npm tarball 4.03 MB, unpacked 14.73 MB — but the ONLY runtime asset is a single `dist/opencv.js` of **13.30 MB** with the wasm base64-embedded (no separate .wasm to trace, which actually SIMPLIFIES Vercel bundling). It is genuine OpenCV 5.0.0 (confirmed via cv.getBuildInformation()).

I ran it under Node 24 on Windows. Measured: `require()` 109 ms, wasm instantiate 44 ms → **~153 ms total cold init**; RSS 106 MB after init, 152 MB peak after a full pipeline. On a 2000x1500 greyscale image: Canny 33 ms, findContours 10 ms (3038 contours), **warpPerspective 56 ms**, adaptiveThreshold(31px Gaussian) 90 ms, connectedComponentsWithStats 22 ms. A Vercel 1-vCPU Lambda will be maybe 1.5–2x slower, so budget ~300 ms init + ~400 ms for a full dewarp+analyse pass. That comfortably fits 2 GB / 300 s.

BREAKING CHANGE vs 4.x: the module is now a **thenable**, not an object with `onRuntimeInitialized`. You must `const cv = await require('@techstark/opencv-js')`. Immediately after `require()`, `cv.Mat` is `undefined` and `Object.keys(cv)` is `[]` — every 4.x tutorial you find will be wrong.
findings.source: model-run benchmark (scripts at D:/tmp equivalents /tmp/pkgprobe/bench2.mjs) + npm registry + package tarball inspection

findings.topic: @techstark/opencv-js — exact runtime API inventory (what is and is not in the default build)
findings.detail:
I enumerated the live module. PRESENT: ORB, MSER, FastFeatureDetector, GFTTDetector, SimpleBlobDetector, BFMatcher, CLAHE, matchTemplate, findHomography, estimateAffine2D, warpPerspective, getPerspectiveTransform, HoughLinesP, adaptiveThreshold, connectedComponentsWithStats, readNetFromONNX (dnn IS included), minAreaRect, approxPolyDP, contourArea, morphologyEx, distanceTransform, watershed, grabCut, inpaint, TrackerMIL, Mat, MatVector, KeyPointVector, DMatchVector, matFromImageData, matFromArray, split, merge, cvtColor, RANSAC, NORM_HAMMING, THRESH_OTSU, ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C.
MISSING: SIFT, AKAZE, BRISK, KAZE, FlannBasedMatcher, estimateAffinePartial2D, goodFeaturesToTrack (use GFTTDetector), phaseCorrelate, fastNlMeansDenoising, Subdiv2D, createCLAHE (use `new cv.CLAHE()`), and **imdecode / imencode — there is no imgcodecs**. `imread`/`imshow` exist but need a DOM canvas, so in a serverless function you must decode JPEG/PNG with sharp to raw RGBA and hand it to `cv.matFromImageData({data,width,height})`, then read pixels back out via `mat.data` into `sharp(buf,{raw:{...}})`. Default upstream whitelist (opencv/platforms/js/opencv_js.config.py) is core, imgproc, objdetect, video, dnn, features, photo, calib3d. A slim imgproc-only build is possible by editing that whitelist and rebuilding with Emscripten in Docker, but no prebuilt slim npm package exists — and given the measured 153 ms init, it is not worth the build-chain maintenance.

findings.topic: opencv-wasm and @u4/opencv4nodejs — both unusable
findings.detail:
`opencv-wasm` 4.3.0-10 (BSD-3-Clause, 17.10 MB unpacked) was last published **2022-05-12** — abandoned for 4 years and pinned to OpenCV 4.3.0. Do not use.
`@u4/opencv4nodejs` 7.1.2 (MIT, 11.35 MB, last modified 2024-09-13) depends on `@u4/opencv-build`, `nan`, and `node-gyp` — it compiles OpenCV from source or links a system OpenCV at install time. There is no prebuilt linux-x64 binary path that survives Vercel's build container, and Vercel explicitly warns that native/node-gyp packages are not guaranteed to be available in the Function environment. Verdict: not viable on Vercel serverless. @techstark/opencv-js is the only realistic OpenCV option.

findings.topic: jscanify 1.4.3 — avoid; its algorithm is weaker than advertised and its deps are hostile to Vercel
findings.detail:
MIT, v1.4.3 published 2026-07-20, 20,460 downloads/wk — so it IS maintained. But: **30.42 MB unpacked / 35 files**, of which ~9 MB is its own vendored `src/opencv.js` (an older 4.x build) and ~20 MB is demo images and docs shipped inside the package. The Node entry (`main: src/jscanify-node.js`) hard-depends on `canvas` ^3.2.3 (node-canvas, native Cairo binary) and `jsdom` ^29.1.1. Both `canvas` and `jsdom` are in Next.js's default `serverExternalPackages` list so they won't be webpack-mangled, but you still ship a native binary plus a full DOM implementation into your Lambda for what is ~120 lines of image code.
More importantly, I read the algorithm: `Canny(img, 50, 200)` → `GaussianBlur(3x3)` → `threshold(OTSU)` → `findContours(RETR_CCOMP, CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)` → largest contour by area → **`cv.minAreaRect(contour)`** → `getPerspectiveTransform` → `warpPerspective`. Because it takes corners from `minAreaRect` (a rotated *rectangle*) rather than `approxPolyDP` to a true quadrilateral, it fundamentally cannot model perspective foreshortening — exactly the failure mode of a hand-held phone photo of a form on a desk. Note also it Cannys *before* blurring, which is backwards. Verdict: reimplement the 120 lines yourself against @techstark/opencv-js with approxPolyDP + a 4-corner quad, and skip the dependency. `react-document-scanner` did not surface as a maintained current package.
findings.source: package tarball inspection of jscanify-1.4.3.tgz (src/jscanify.js, package.json) + npm registry

findings.topic: image-js 1.7.0 — the sleeper find: pure-TypeScript homography warp + ORB, MIT, zero wasm
findings.detail:
MIT, v1.7.0 published 2026-07-08, 48,891 downloads/wk, 12.53 MB unpacked, pure TypeScript (deps are all pure-JS: ml-matrix, ml-ransac, ml-affine-transform, ml-convolution, fast-png, jpeg-js, ts-pattern). Runs identically in Node and the browser. Relevant modules: `geometry` → **getPerspectiveWarp(pts, {width,height})** which computes a true homography via SVD (ml-matrix SingularValueDecomposition) and is explicitly documented for "a document photographed at an angle", plus `transform(matrix, {interpolationType:'nearest'|'bilinear'|'bicubic', borderType, inverse, fullImage})` which accepts **2x3 OR 3x3** matrices. `featureMatching` → getFastKeypoints, getOrientedFastKeypoints, getBriefDescriptors, getHarrisScore, getShiTomasiScore, bruteForceMatch, getCrosscheckMatches — i.e. a complete ORB pipeline in pure TS, and `ml-ransac` is already a dependency for robust homography fitting. `roi` → fromMask, computeRois, getRois, Roi, RoiMapManager, waterShed (connected components with per-blob stats). `morphology` → erode, dilate, open, close, topHat, bottomHat, morphologicalGradient, clearBorder, cannyEdgeDetector, floodFill. `operations` → threshold with 13 global algorithms (otsu, huang, intermodes, isodata, li, mean, minimum, moments, percentile, shanbhag, triangle, yen), correctBackground (2D polynomial regression shading correction — directly useful for uneven phone-flash illumination), extract, crop, cropAlpha, split/merge, convertColor.
API GOTCHA: points are `{column, row}`, NOT `{x, y}`. Passing {x,y} silently yields NaN width/height and a confusing RangeError deep inside Image.createFrom.
Measured by me on 2000x1500 grey, Node 24: import 251 ms (slower to load than OpenCV.js!), **perspective transform 70 ms** (vs OpenCV's 56 ms — competitive, the JIT handles the per-pixel loop well), otsu threshold 13 ms, fromMask+getRois 76 ms, FAST keypoints 145 ms, but **cannyEdgeDetector 513 ms (15x slower than OpenCV's 33 ms)**. Peak RSS 318 MB, roughly 2x OpenCV.js.

findings.topic: wasm-vips 0.0.18 — the only JS route to true nonlinear dewarp (curved/creased paper)
findings.detail:
MIT, v0.0.18 published 2026-06-09, 63,845 downloads/wk, 12.50 MB unpacked but the core runtime is just **vips.wasm at 5.08 MB** (optional vips-heif 3.48 MB / vips-jxl 2.17 MB / vips-resvg 1.16 MB can be omitted). Dual CJS/ESM, separate browser and node entry points. This is real libvips compiled with Emscripten, and unlike sharp it exposes the operations sharp omits — I confirmed in vips.d.ts: **mapim(index, {interpolate, background, premultiplied})** (arbitrary per-pixel source-coordinate remap → lets you implement both an exact homography AND a nonlinear dewarp of a curved/creased page, which nothing else in the JS ecosystem gives you), plus quadratic(), affine(), similarity(), canny(), sobel(), houghLine() (skew estimation), findTrim(), labelregions() (connected components), morph(), rank(), convsep(), matrixinvert(), profile(), project().
TWO REAL CAVEATS. (1) In the **browser it requires SharedArrayBuffer**, so the page must be cross-origin isolated with `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` and `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`. That is a genuine architectural cost: COEP:require-corp will break loading Supabase Storage images, Groq responses rendered as images, third-party embeds, and analytics scripts unless every one of them serves CORP/CORS headers. (2) The README still carries a maintainer note: "This library is still under early development." Requires Node >= 17 / Chrome 95 / Firefox 100 / Safari 16.4 (wasm SIMD + exception handling). In Node (server-side) neither caveat bites — SharedArrayBuffer is unconditionally available.
findings.source: package tarball inspection of wasm-vips-0.0.18.tgz (lib/vips.d.ts, package.json, README.md) + npm registry

findings.topic: tesseract.js 7.0.0 — genuinely good for the narrow label-anchor job, useless for handwriting
findings.detail:
Apache-2.0, v7.0.0 published 2025-12-15, 2.67M downloads/wk. Package itself is only 1.41 MB; the weight is the separately-CDN-fetched core and language data. Real sizes I pulled from jsDelivr for tesseract.js-core@7.0.0: tesseract-core-simd-lstm.wasm **2.73 MB** (smallest usable — LSTM-only + SIMD), tesseract-core-simd.wasm 3.29 MB (LSTM+legacy), plus new `relaxedsimd` variants. Language data: eng.traineddata.gz in the default `4.0.0_best_int` set is **2.95 MB** gzipped (the `4.0.0` LSTM+legacy set is 10.92 MB). So a browser-side label-anchor pass costs ~5.7 MB on first load, then it is cached in IndexedDB (the package depends on idb-keyval). v7 cut runtimes 15–35% vs v6 via the relaxedsimd build; you must point `corePath` at a DIRECTORY, not a specific .js, or it cannot pick the right variant.
WORD-LEVEL OUTPUT: yes, fully. `Word` = `{ text, confidence: number, bbox: {x0,y0,x1,y1}, symbols: Symbol[], choices: Choice[], font_name }`, nested Page > Block > Paragraph > Line > Word > Symbol, and every level carries its own `confidence` and `bbox`. **But `blocks` defaults to `false`** (worker-script/constants/defaultOutput.js) and `page.blocks` is `null` unless you call `recognize(img, opts, { blocks: true })`. Other useful knobs: `rectangle: {top,left,width,height}` to OCR only a sub-region (perfect for scanning just the label band you expect), `rotateAuto`, `tessedit_pageseg_mode` (PSM), `tessedit_char_whitelist`, `user_defined_dpi`, and output flags `imageGrey` / `imageBinary` which hand you Tesseract's own Otsu-binarised image for free.
HANDWRITING: the official Tesseract FAQ is blunt — "You can, but it won't work very well, as Tesseract is designed for printed text." Do not use it for the handwritten values; that stays with the Groq VLM. For the proposed narrow job — locating printed anchors like "Signature", "Affix Photo", "Thumb Impression" on a fixed template so you can register geometry — it is well suited, because those are clean printed words, you can constrain PSM and whitelist, and you get per-word bbox + confidence.

findings.topic: ONNX Runtime on Vercel — node vs web, and the Large Functions escape hatch
findings.detail:
Both at v1.29.0, MIT, published 2026-08-24 (very actively maintained). `onnxruntime-node` unpacks to **296 MB** because it ships prebuilts for every platform in one tarball — but the linux/x64 slice you actually need is only libonnxruntime.so.1 (44.73 MB) + onnxruntime_binding.node (389 KB) ≈ 45 MB. It IS already in Next.js's default `serverExternalPackages` list (alongside sharp, canvas, jsdom, @huggingface/transformers), so Next will `require()` it natively rather than webpack it. To make it work you need (a) `npm install --arch=x64 --platform=linux onnxruntime-node` at build time, and (b) `outputFileTracingIncludes` pinned to `node_modules/onnxruntime-node/bin/napi-v6/linux/x64/**` with the other platforms excluded, or you blow the 250 MB limit. The well-documented failure mode is `libonnxruntime.so.1: cannot open shared object file`, which bites especially via @huggingface/transformers because its backend auto-detection prefers native bindings; the published workaround is `env.backends.setPriority(['wasm','cpu'])`.
`onnxruntime-web` unpacks to 142 MB but the assets you actually ship are `ort-wasm-simd-threaded.wasm` (**13.96 MB**, non-JSEP CPU) or the jsep/WebGPU build (27.80 MB), plus `ort.bundle.min.mjs` (413 KB) or `ort.wasm.min.mjs` (~578 KB). It runs fine inside a Vercel Node function too and sidesteps the native-binary problem entirely at some CPU cost.
DECISIVE NEW FACT: Vercel now offers **Large Functions (beta) with 5 GB uncompressed bundles** on the Node.js runtime — requires fluid compute with Active CPU, opt in per-project with `VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_FUNCTIONS=1`. Only functions exceeding 250 MB use the large path. That removes the size objection to onnxruntime-node + a couple of models entirely (not available with Secure Compute / Static IPs).

findings.topic: Signature-detection models: the good one is AGPL, the licence-safe one needs a 10-minute export
findings.detail:
`tech4humans/yolov8s-signature-detector` is the best-known and best-performing (P 94.74%, R 89.72%, mAP@50 94.50%, mAP@50-95 67.35%, 171.56 ms on ONNX Runtime CPU; yolov8s.onnx = 42.5 MB, yolov8s.pt = 21.5 MB) — but it is **AGPL-3.0**, inherited from Ultralytics YOLOv8. For a hosted multi-tenant SaaS, AGPL §13 requires offering your platform's corresponding source to every user who interacts with it over the network. Treat as a hard blocker.
LICENCE-SAFE ALTERNATIVES (all Apache-2.0 / MIT):
• `mdefrance/yolos-tiny-signature-detection` — **Apache-2.0**, model.safetensors 24.7 MB, 1,842 downloads/30d. YOLOS is ViT-based (hustvl/yolos-tiny, Apache-2.0), so no Ultralytics contamination. No ONNX in the repo, but `Xenova/yolos-tiny` shows what the exported sizes look like: model.onnx 25.0 MB, model_quantized/uint8 ~9.2 MB, model_q4f16 6.7 MB. Export once with Optimum and you have a ~7–9 MB detector that runs in transformers.js in the browser or in a Lambda. This is the recommendation.
• `mdefrance/yolos-small-signature-detection` — Apache-2.0, 116.9 MB safetensors, better accuracy.
• `tech4humans/conditional-detr-50-signature-detector` — **Apache-2.0**, 166 MB safetensors, 3,232 downloads/30d, the same team's non-AGPL alternative.
• `onnx-community/yolos-base-signature-detection-ONNX` — Apache-2.0 and ONNX-ready for transformers.js, but yolos-base is huge: model.onnx 487.5 MB, int8/uint8/quantized 236.2 MB, q4f16 198.1 MB. Too heavy.
• `Miracle12345/conditionaldetr_signature_detection` and `vikramkishore/yolov8-signature-detection` are tagged MIT but have 0 downloads — unvetted, and the latter's MIT tag on YOLOv8-derived weights is legally doubtful.

findings.topic: DocLayout-YOLO has a real licence conflict — do not ship it without legal review
findings.detail: The HuggingFace weights repos (`juliozhao/DocLayout-YOLO-DocStructBench` 38.8 MB .pt; `wybxc/DocLayout-YOLO-DocStructBench-onnx` 71.8 MB .onnx; `darknoah99/...`; `anyformat/doclayout-yolo-docstructbench`) all carry `license: apache-2.0` in their model cards. But the upstream source repo `opendatalab/DocLayout-YOLO` on GitHub is licensed **AGPL-3.0** and its own README acknowledges "The code base is built with ultralytics and YOLO-v10" — YOLOv10 and Ultralytics are both AGPL-3.0. An Apache-2.0 tag on a model card does not launder an AGPL-3.0 derivative. Same pattern applies to `Armaggheddon/yolo26-document-layout` and `Armaggheddon/yolo11-document-layout`, both tagged **MIT** with attractively small weights (yolo26n 5.3 MB, yolo11n 5.4 MB, yolo26m 42.2 MB) and real traction (2,415 and 860 downloads/30d) — but they are Ultralytics-trained. `Oblix/yolov10m-doclaynet_ONNX_document-layout-analysis` (58.7 MB, transformers.js-ready) has no licence declared at all. Note that Ultralytics' claim that AGPL propagates to weights produced by their trainer is contested and untested in court, but it is an unresolved risk you should decide about deliberately rather than by accident.
findings.source: https://github.com/opendatalab/DocLayout-YOLO (LICENSE: AGPL-3.0) vs https://huggingface.co/wybxc/DocLayout-YOLO-DocStructBench-onnx (cardData license: apache-2.0); HF API for the Armaggheddon and Oblix repos

findings.topic: SlimSAM via transformers.js — 13 MB, Apache-2.0, box-promptable pixel-accurate masks
findings.detail: `Xenova/slimsam-77-uniform` — **Apache-2.0**, `library_name: transformers.js`, 50,017 downloads/30d. Split into two ONNX graphs: vision_encoder (22.2 MB fp32 / 11.6 MB fp16 / **8.5 MB quantized**) and prompt_encoder_mask_decoder (15.8 MB fp32 / 8.2 MB fp16 / **4.7 MB quantized**) — so **13.2 MB total quantized**. This is directly relevant to the stated #1 priority: rather than asking a VLM for pixel coordinates, you feed SAM a coarse box prompt derived from your stored per-template geometry and it returns a pixel-accurate mask of the pasted photograph, from which you take an exact tight crop. It handles the awkward real-world cases well — a crooked photo overlapping the printed box border, staple marks, a photocopy-of-a-photo with low contrast — because it segments by appearance, not by finding the printed rectangle. Runs in the browser (free compute, no upload) or in a Lambda. Upstream `Zigeng/SlimSAM-uniform-77` is also Apache-2.0. `Xenova/slimsam-50-uniform` is a smaller variant. MobileSAM alternatives exist (`qualcomm/MobileSam` Apache-2.0) but are not packaged for transformers.js.

findings.topic: Background removal / ink isolation in Node — every convenient option is licence-blocked, and they are the wrong tool anyway
findings.detail:
`@imgly/background-removal-node` 1.4.5: the LICENSE.md in imgly/background-removal-js is the **GNU Affero General Public License v3** (npm reports 'SEE LICENSE IN LICENSE.md', which is why it looks permissive at a glance). Commercial use requires a paid IMG.LY agreement. It also pins `sharp: ~0.32.4`, three minor versions behind your 0.35.3, which will fight your own sharp install. Models are ~44 MB (small) / ~88 MB (medium) / ~176 MB (large), fetched from IMG.LY's servers at first run. Blocker.
`briaai/RMBG-1.4` (onnx/model_quantized.onnx 42.3 MB, 443k downloads/30d) is `license: other`, `license_name: bria-rmbg-1.4`, gated, and commercial use requires an agreement at bria.ai. Same for RMBG-2.0. Blocker.
MIT alternatives exist but are heavy: `onnx-community/BiRefNet_lite-ONNX` is **MIT** but model.onnx is 213.6 MB / fp16 109.2 MB. `onnx-community/BiRefNet-ONNX`, `-portrait-ONNX`, `-DIS5K-ONNX` likewise MIT. U²-Net weights are Apache-2.0 and rembg's code is MIT — but rembg is Python, and `rembg-node` is explicitly disavowed by its own author as unmaintained with missing algorithms.
HONEST VERDICT: all of these are *salient-object / portrait matting* models. Ink isolation on a form scan is a different problem — you want illumination-corrected local binarisation, not semantic segmentation. Do it with primitives you already have: CLAHE (sharp `.clahe()` or `new cv.CLAHE()`) → background division / `image-js` `correctBackground()` (2D polynomial shading fit) → `cv.adaptiveThreshold(ADAPTIVE_THRESH_GAUSSIAN_C)` (90 ms measured on 2000x1500) or an image-js global threshold after correction → `morphologyEx` open to kill speckle → `connectedComponentsWithStats` to keep ink blobs and drop photocopier noise. For separating blue/black ink from a printed line, `sharp.recomb()` or a per-channel `linear()` in HSV/LAB gets you a chroma-based ink mask far more cheaply than any 42 MB network. Tesseract.js's `imageBinary` output is a free second opinion.

findings.topic: Vercel platform constraints that will shape the architecture regardless of library choice
findings.detail:
From the current Vercel Functions limits page (last_updated 2026-07-01): bundle **250 MB uncompressed** standard, **5 GB via Large Functions beta** (Node.js/Bun/Python, needs fluid compute + Active CPU, opt in with `VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_FUNCTIONS=1`, unavailable with Secure Compute/Static IPs). Memory **2 GB / 1 vCPU on Hobby (max)**, 2 GB default and **4 GB / 2 vCPU max on Pro**. Max duration 300 s default on both, 800 s max on Pro, 1800 s extended beta. Concurrency auto-scales to 30,000.
TWO THINGS THAT WILL BITE YOU: (1) **Request and response body are capped at 4.5 MB** (`FUNCTION_PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE`). A modern phone photo of an A4 form is routinely 4–12 MB, so staff uploads MUST go browser → Supabase Storage via a signed URL, and the function receives only the object key. This also means any returned crops should be written to Storage, not returned inline as base64. (2) Functions default to region **iad1**; you must explicitly set bom1, and note multi-region is Pro/Enterprise only. Also 1,024 file descriptors shared across concurrent executions.
On bundling: `sharp`, `onnxruntime-node`, `canvas`, `jsdom`, `@huggingface/transformers`, and `@xenova/transformers` are ALL already in Next.js 16's default `serverExternalPackages` list, so they are `require()`d natively rather than webpacked — you do not need to configure that. You DO need `outputFileTracingIncludes` for any .wasm or .onnx you load by constructed path, since Next's tracer cannot follow those. Note `vercel.json` `includeFiles`/`excludeFiles` do NOT work in Next.js — use `outputFileTracingIncludes`/`Excludes`.

findings.topic: @techstark/opencv-js in a Next.js build — the fs/path/crypto resolution issue
findings.detail: The Emscripten glue in opencv.js references Node built-ins (`fs`, `path`, `crypto`) so it can locate a wasm file on disk. When webpack compiles it for the client target those requires fail with "Module not found: Can't resolve 'fs'". The package README's own fix is `resolve.fallback = { fs: false, path: false, crypto: false }`. In Next.js 16 this goes in the `webpack` hook guarded on `!isServer` (or better, keyed off `nextRuntime === undefined`), and you must SPREAD the existing `config.resolve.fallback` rather than replacing `config.resolve`, or you destroy Next's own aliases. The cleaner answer for a server-only pipeline is to never let it into the client graph at all: import it only inside Route Handlers / Server Components, and if you also want a browser copy, load it with `dynamic(() => import(...), { ssr: false })` or from a CDN. Caveat: I found no bug report specific to @techstark/opencv-js failing on Vercel — this is the general Next.js pattern applied to the package's documented requirement, not a reproduced Vercel failure.

Also noted: jimp 1.6.1 (MIT, 3.31 MB, 2026-04-07) is pure-JS but much weaker than image-js for CV; @napi-rs/canvas 1.0.8 (MIT, 2026-08-24) is a far better server-side canvas than node-canvas if you ever need one.

recommendations: Treat sharp as a decoder/encoder/colour-pipeline, not as your CV engine. It cannot do the one transform this product depends on (4-point perspective correction), and trim() cannot find a pasted photo. Use it for: EXIF autoOrient, downscale with lanczos3, clahe() for illumination, linear()/recomb() for ink chroma isolation, extract() for the final crops, raw({depth:'uchar'}) in/out as the zero-copy bridge to whatever CV library you pick, and final JPEG/WebP encoding.

Adopt @techstark/opencv-js 5.0.0-release.1 as the server-side CV engine. I measured it: 153 ms cold init, 13.3 MB single self-contained JS (no separate .wasm to trace, so Vercel bundling is trivial), 152 MB peak RSS, warpPerspective on 2000x1500 in 56 ms. The 'opencv-wasm is too heavy for Vercel' assumption in the brief is wrong for this package. Write `const cv = await require('@techstark/opencv-js')` — 5.0 returns a thenable and every 4.x onRuntimeInitialized example will silently give you an empty object.

Build the photo/signature localisation on template registration, not on VLM coordinates — and OpenCV.js already ships everything you need: ORB + BFMatcher(NORM_HAMMING) + findHomography(RANSAC) to register each new scan against the admin's stored blank template, then warpPerspective the scan into template space, then read the crops straight out of the stored per-field rectangles. Because the layout is fixed per organisation, this is a solved geometry problem, and it degrades gracefully: report the RANSAC inlier ratio as your per-crop confidence and emit 'Not Detected' below a threshold. Note SIFT/AKAZE/BRISK and FlannBasedMatcher are NOT in the build — plan on ORB + brute-force.

Layer Xenova/slimsam-77-uniform (Apache-2.0, 13.2 MB quantized, transformers.js) on top of the registered geometry for the pasted photograph specifically. Feed it a coarse box prompt from the template rectangle and take a pixel-accurate mask back. This is what makes a crooked, border-overlapping, stapled, photocopied passport photo crop correctly, and it never invents a box because a low mask IoU against the expected rectangle is a clean 'Not Detected' signal. This directly addresses the stated #1 priority far better than asking a VLM for pixels.

For the signature detector, do NOT use tech4humans/yolov8s-signature-detector — it is AGPL-3.0 via Ultralytics and §13 network copyleft is fatal for a hosted SaaS. Export mdefrance/yolos-tiny-signature-detection (Apache-2.0, 24.7 MB safetensors) to ONNX with Optimum and quantize; Xenova/yolos-tiny shows the target sizes (~9.2 MB uint8, 6.7 MB q4f16). Budget half a day for the export and a validation pass on your own Indian-form samples. Get legal eyes on DocLayout-YOLO and the Armaggheddon MIT-tagged YOLO weights before shipping either — the model cards and the upstream repo licences contradict each other.

Use tesseract.js 7.0.0 exactly as scoped in the brief — printed label anchors only, never handwriting. The official Tesseract FAQ says handwriting 'won't work very well'. Run it client-side (2.73 MB simd-lstm wasm + 2.95 MB eng data, IndexedDB-cached), pass `output: { blocks: true }` because blocks defaults to false, and use the `rectangle` option to OCR only the narrow band where you expect 'Signature' / 'Affix Photo' / 'Thumb Impression'. Word.bbox {x0,y0,x1,y1} + Word.confidence give you the anchor points to seed or verify the homography, and Word.choices gives you a cheap ambiguity signal.

Do the perspective correction in the BROWSER before upload, and make this decision early because it interacts with a hard platform limit: Vercel caps request bodies at 4.5 MB, and phone photos of A4 forms are routinely 4–12 MB. Staff must upload to Supabase Storage via a signed URL regardless — so put corner detection and the warp client-side (free compute, smaller upload, instant user feedback on a bad capture), then upload only the rectified page. image-js (MIT, pure TS, no wasm, no COOP/COEP requirement) is the right choice here: getPerspectiveWarp + transform measured 70 ms on 2000x1500, competitive with OpenCV's 56 ms. Just avoid its cannyEdgeDetector (513 ms, 15x slower than OpenCV) — do edge detection on a heavily downscaled proxy, or use OpenCV.js in a worker.

Watch the {column,row} vs {x,y} trap in image-js. Its Point type is {column, row}; passing {x, y} produces NaN dimensions and a RangeError thrown deep inside Image.createFrom with no hint about the real cause. I hit this directly. Wrap it in a typed adapter at your module boundary.

Skip jscanify entirely. It drags in node-canvas (native) + jsdom, ships 30 MB including demo images, vendors its own stale 9 MB OpenCV 4.x, and its detection is Canny→blur→Otsu→largest contour→minAreaRect — a rotated *rectangle*, which structurally cannot represent perspective foreshortening. That is precisely your dominant input condition. Reimplement its ~120 lines with approxPolyDP to a true 4-point quad; you will get better results with fewer dependencies.

Keep wasm-vips (MIT, 5.08 MB wasm) in reserve for one specific job the rest of the stack cannot do: nonlinear dewarp of curved/creased paper, via its mapim() operation. It is the only JS library exposing an arbitrary per-pixel remap. Use it SERVER-SIDE only — in the browser it requires SharedArrayBuffer and therefore COOP/COEP cross-origin isolation, which will break your Supabase Storage image loads and third-party scripts unless every one of them serves CORP headers. Also note its README still says 'under early development'.

For ink isolation, do not reach for a background-removal model. @imgly is AGPL-3.0 (and pins sharp 0.32.4, conflicting with your 0.35.3), briaai/RMBG is a proprietary Bria licence, and the MIT BiRefNet ONNX is 109–213 MB. They are portrait-matting models solving a different problem. CLAHE → background division (image-js correctBackground, or divide by a heavily-blurred copy) → adaptiveThreshold(GAUSSIAN_C) (90 ms measured) → morphologyEx open → connectedComponentsWithStats gets you cleaner ink masks, at zero licence risk and ~1000x less weight.

Prefer onnxruntime-web (13.96 MB wasm) over onnxruntime-node in Vercel functions unless you measure a real need for the native speed. onnxruntime-node's documented Vercel failure is `libonnxruntime.so.1: cannot open shared object file`, and making it work needs `npm install --arch=x64 --platform=linux`, outputFileTracingIncludes pinned to bin/napi-v6/linux/x64/** and the other 250 MB of platforms excluded. If you do need native, note Vercel's Large Functions beta now allows 5 GB bundles (VERCEL_SUPPORT_LARGE_FUNCTIONS=1, requires fluid compute + Active CPU) — that removes the size objection but not the fragility.

Set the region to bom1 explicitly — Vercel functions default to iad1, and for Indian staff uploading multi-megabyte photos the round-trip difference is large and user-visible. Multi-region is Pro/Enterprise only.
caveats: My performance numbers for @techstark/opencv-js and image-js are real measurements I ran, but on a Windows dev machine under Node 24, not on Vercel. A Vercel 1-vCPU Fluid instance will likely be 1.5–2x slower and has a cold-start component I could not measure. Treat the numbers as relative comparisons (OpenCV Canny is 15x faster than image-js Canny; the two perspective warps are within 25% of each other) rather than as absolute latency budgets. Re-benchmark on a real preview deployment before committing.

The benchmark input was a synthetic 2000x1500 greyscale image with a regular sparse pattern, not a real photographed form. Timings for warpPerspective, Canny and adaptiveThreshold are representative because they are data-independent; the findContours contour count (3038) and the image-js ROI count (1) are artifacts of the synthetic input and mean nothing.

I did not find a bug report of @techstark/opencv-js specifically failing on Vercel. The webpack fs/path/crypto guidance is the package's own documented requirement combined with standard Next.js practice, not a reproduced deployment failure. Verify on a preview deploy.

Ultralytics' position that AGPL-3.0 propagates from their training code to the resulting model weights is contested and, as far as I know, untested in court. I have reported the licence conflicts factually (upstream repo AGPL vs model card Apache/MIT) because they are real and unresolved, but I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. The DocLayout-YOLO and Armaggheddon YOLO weights specifically need a decision from someone who is.

I did not benchmark tesseract.js accuracy on actual Indian paper forms, nor did I test its behaviour on Devanagari labels — the brief mentions Hindi labels, and that needs a separate `hin` traineddata (additional download, and Devanagari accuracy in Tesseract is materially worse than Latin). Verify against your own samples.

I did not verify onnxruntime-web or SlimSAM actually running end-to-end inside a Vercel function or the browser; sizes and licences are confirmed from the registries but the integration is unproven here.

The claim that Vercel functions have a writable /tmp of up to 500 MB came from a secondary blog source, not Vercel's own limits page, which does not mention it. Confirm before relying on /tmp for model caching.

Package sizes I quote as 'unpacked' are npm's dist.unpackedSize for the whole tarball, which includes types, docs and demo assets. Where it mattered (opencv.js at 13.3 MB, vips.wasm at 5.08 MB, the tesseract core variants, the ort wasm variants) I inspected the actual tarball and quoted the specific runtime file instead — those are the numbers to budget against.

The Xenova/* model repos (slimsam, yolos-tiny, trocr) do not declare a licence field on HuggingFace; I inferred permissiveness from the upstream base models (Zigeng/SlimSAM-uniform-77 and hustvl/yolos-tiny are both Apache-2.0). Confirm the conversion repos' terms before shipping.
